lesson.title: Splitting the Feast: How Similar Species Coexist Through Resource Partitioning
lesson.summary: Resource partitioning is the process by which competing species divide a shared resource along some dimension, such as location, timing, or diet, allowing them to reduce competition enough to coexist.
lesson.body:
The competitive exclusion principle predicts that two species competing for the exact same resource in the exact same way cannot coexist indefinitely. Yet forests are full of insect eating birds, coral reefs are full of similarly shaped fish, and grasslands are full of grazing mammals, all living together for generations. Resource partitioning is the main reason this is possible. Rather than using a shared resource in an identical way, competing species divide it up, by feeding at different times, in different places, on slightly different foods, or in different ways, so that the overlap in what they actually need is reduced. Once the overlap is small enough, direct competition eases and coexistence becomes stable.

One of the classic demonstrations of this comes from the ecologist Robert MacArthur's study of warblers in the spruce forests of the northeastern United States, published in 1958. Five species of wood warblers, all small insect eating songbirds, appeared at first glance to be doing the same job in the same trees. But when MacArthur carefully recorded where in each spruce tree the different warbler species spent their time foraging, he found consistent differences. Some species concentrated their feeding near the top of the tree, others foraged mainly in the middle, and others worked lower branches or the outer edges of the foliage. Each species also tended to move and hunt for insects in a somewhat different way. The birds were partitioning the tree, dividing up the physical space and foraging behavior, which reduced how directly they competed for the same insects even though they shared the same forest.

Resource partitioning can happen along several different dimensions, and ecologists often group them into a few broad categories. Spatial partitioning means using different physical locations, as with the warblers foraging at different heights. Temporal partitioning means using the same resource at different times, such as one species of owl hunting at dusk while another hunts well after midnight. Partitioning by resource type means specializing on somewhat different food items or other resources, such as two seed eating finches with beaks suited to different sized seeds. Any of these differences can be enough to let competing species avoid the head to head, identical resource use that the competitive exclusion principle warns against.

It is worth being honest that resource partitioning is not always a clean or complete solution. Species can still compete somewhat even with partitioning in place, particularly when a resource becomes especially scarce, such as during a drought or a harsh winter, and overlap that seemed small in good times can become significant when resources are tight. Ecologists also debate, for any particular pair of species, how much of the observed difference in resource use is truly a response to competition versus simply a preexisting difference in each species' biology. Even with those caveats, resource partitioning remains one of the best supported explanations for why so many similar species manage to share the same habitat rather than following the stark, one winner outcome that strict competitive exclusion would predict.
